Hi all,

I recently saw the paper A Rocq Formalization of Simplicial Lagrange Finite Elements:

https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20345

As far as I understand, the paper formalizes the notion of a finite element as a Rocq record, including the cell geometry, the polynomial approximation space, the degrees of freedom, and the required validity proofs, in particular unisolvence. It then instantiates this record for simplicial Lagrange finite elements with evenly distributed nodes, for arbitrary dimension and polynomial degree.

I was wondering whether anything similar has already been done, or is currently being developed, in Lean/mathlib. I know mathlib has some infrastructure for Lagrange interpolation, affine spaces, finite-dimensional vector spaces, and multivariate polynomials, but I am not aware of a formalized finite element structure in the FEM sense.

If this has not been done yet, would it be reasonable to try to port or re-develop this Rocq formalization in Lean? More specifically, would the right starting point be:

  1. defining a general finite element record (K, P, Σ) in Lean,

  2. formalizing simplices and affine reference cells,

  3. defining simplicial Lagrange nodes and degrees of freedom,

  4. proving unisolvence for arbitrary dimension and polynomial degree?

I would be very interested in this direction because it seems like a natural first step toward formal proofs of scientific computing programs, especially finite element codes. Any pointers, existing Lean projects, or advice on which parts of mathlib would be most relevant would be greatly appreciated.
